explanations.answer: What is left of the night
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The voice calls, "Watchman, what is left of the night?" (Isaiah 21:11). And it asks it twice, like the question can't wait. I think whoever is asking really wants to know how long the dark will last.

explanations.answer: Who is coming up the road
explanations.explanation: Good guess, because a watchman does watch for travelers. But the voice from Seir never asks about anyone on the road. It asks, "Watchman, what is left of the night?" (Isaiah 21:11). The question is about the night itself.

I get it, friend. Watchmen and enemies go together like dough and a hot oven. But this passage never mentions an attack. The voice asks, "Watchman, what is left of the night?" (Isaiah 21:11), and that's the whole question.

Close, but half an answer is still half an answer. The watchman says, "Morning has come, but also the night." (Isaiah 21:12). So morning is there, and the night is right there with it. Don't drop the second half, baker!

Yes, friend! The watchman says, "Morning has come, but also the night." (Isaiah 21:12). He doesn't give just one or the other. He gives both, and he leaves it there. I'd be asking a follow-up question too.

You've got it, baker. After "If you would inquire, then inquire," the watchman says, "Come back yet again." (Isaiah 21:12). So the door stays open for another visit. I know a little about waiting around for somebody to come back, and I like that invitation.

Not quite, friend. That would be a slammed door, and the watchman doesn't do that. He says, "If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again." (Isaiah 21:12). The invitation is to return, not to leave.

I can see why you picked it, since the whole passage is about the night. But the watchman never says to wait for dawn. His words are "If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again." (Isaiah 21:12). He tells the voice to come back.
